I have been farming these 12 mu in Quzhou for 40 years, and I know every piece of this land. It is early spring now, and the winter wheat I sowed last October is waking up from dormancy. With the well on my farm, I do not worry about drought, so I can manage both crops intensively.

For my wheat, I planted an improved variety at about 15 kg per mu last autumn after rotary tillage. The crop looks even and healthy. Now I will topdress with urea at green-up and again at jointing — altogether about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu for the season. I also apply compound fertilizer with phosphorus and potassium at basal, around 6 kg phosphorus and 4 kg potassium per mu. I already irrigated once before winter to protect the seedlings from freezing, and this spring I will irrigate two more times: once at jointing and once at grain filling. That makes three irrigations in total. For pests, I will spray herbicide once in early spring, insecticide twice when aphids and armyworms appear, and fungicide once at heading to prevent powdery mildew — four applications in total. If the weather cooperates, I expect about 520 kg per mu.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I will immediately plant hybrid maize — I like varieties such as Nongda 372 because they yield well and resist lodging. I will use no-tillage to save time and keep moisture, sowing about 2.5 kg per mu. For fertilizer, I will apply 15 kg nitrogen, 5 kg phosphorus, and 4 kg potassium per mu, split between basal and the big trumpet stage. I will irrigate twice: once if June is dry after sowing, and once at the tasseling-silking stage, which is the critical period. For pests, I will apply herbicide once before emergence, insecticide twice for corn borers and spider mites, and skip fungicide unless the season is unusually wet — three applications total. With good management, I expect about 580 kg per mu from the maize.

I manage this way because 40 years of experience and my schooling have taught me that steady, timely inputs beat heavy, lazy applications. I do not waste money on excessive fertilizer, but I do not starve my crops either. The double-cropping system here is tight — wheat to maize in just a few days — so no-tillage for maize and reliable irrigation from my well are the keys to making both crops succeed on the same 12 mu.
